sites.desc: The largest Ubaid-period settlement discovered outside Mesopotamia. Bahra 1 is a sprawling site in the Al-Subiyah desert that served as a major center for shell ornament production and trade during the late 6th millennium BC. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) established that during the Ubaid period, the coastline was 1.5 km south of Bahra 1, and the site lay further inland from the sea than the fishing village of H3. The Bahra anticline — a domal structure related to Precambrian Hormuz salt tectonics — has caused tectonic uplift of 1.72–2.64 mm/yr in this area.
sites.ad: Bahra 1 is one of the most significant Ubaid-period settlements discovered outside Mesopotamia. Located on the Al-Subiyah coast north of Kuwait Bay, discovered in 2009 by the Kuwaiti-Polish Archaeological Mission. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) established that during the Ubaid 2/3 period, the site lay inland from the coast, while H3 occupied a narrow peninsula closer to the sea. The settlement contains multi-room stone architecture, extensive Ubaid pottery assemblages, and evidence of long-distance trade networks extending to Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley.
sites.sig: Largest Ubaid settlement outside Mesopotamia; evidence of the earliest cultural exchange networks between Southern Mesopotamia and Eastern Arabia across the Arabian Gulf. Radiocarbon dating of marine shells from the paleo-seabed confirms the mid-Holocene highstand reached this area.
sites.ex: Kuwaiti-Polish Archaeological Mission (KPAM), Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology, University of Warsaw
disc: Shell Crafting Workshop: A 7,700-year-old courtyard used for crafting shell ornaments, the oldest known specialized workshop of its kind in the Gulf region.
Ancient Kilns: More than 20 ancient kilns dating to approximately 7,700 years ago, providing evidence of early pyrotechnology and pottery production.
Owl Sculpture: A rare ancient owl sculpture, one of the earliest artistic representations found in the Arabian Peninsula.
Copper Pin Fragment: An extremely rare copper pin fragment, evidence of early metallurgy and longdistance trade with copper-producing regions.
Ubaid Pottery: Distinctive painted pottery with geometric patterns characteristic of the Ubaid culture, linking this site to Mesopotamian traditions.

Paleo-Seabed Shells: Radiocarbon-dated marine mollusk shells from the paleo-seabed south of Bahra 1, confirming the mid-Holocene highstand reached this area around 5700 BP (Rutkowski & Kiersnowski, 2025).

sites.desc: H3 is located on Jazirat Dubaji, a low peninsula on the north side of Kuwait Bay. During the Ubaid 2/3 period (turn of the 6th and 5th millennia BC), the sea bordered this fishing village on a narrow peninsula, while Bahra 1 lay further inland (Rutkowski & Kiersnowski, 2025). The site is a cultural borderland between Mesopotamian and Arabian Neolithic traditions, yielding some of the most significant maritime archaeological finds in human history.
sites.ad: H3 is located on Jazirat Dubaji, a low peninsula on the north side of Kuwait Bay. During the Ubaid 2/3 period, the sea bordered this fishing village on a narrow peninsula. The site is a cultural borderland between Mesopotamian and Arabian Neolithic traditions, yielding some of the most significant maritime archaeological finds in human history.
sites.sig: Contains the world’s earliest evidence for seagoing vessels and the oldest evidence for the use of masts and sails, fundamentally changing our understanding of prehistoric maritime technology.
sites.ex: Kuwaiti-British Archaeological Expedition, directed by Dr. Harriet Crawford (1998–2004)
disc: World’s Earliest Boat Evidence: Bitumen pieces with barnacles on one side and reed impressions on the other — the earliest physical evidence for actual boats in Western Asia and seagoing vessels globally.
Reed-Bundle Boat Model: A detailed ceramic model of a reed-bundle boat with incisions mimicking reed bundles, more detailed than any similar Mesopotamian find.
Oldest Sail Evidence: A ceramic disc depicting a reed-bundle boat with two masts — the oldest evidence for the use of masts and sails in human history.
Date Stones: Among the earliest evidence of date palm cultivation, connecting to similar finds on Dalma Island in the UAE.

sites.desc: A vast tumulus burial field stretching across the northern coast of Kuwait Bay, containing approximately 130 stone burial mounds and associated structures. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) established that tumuli are distributed along terraces parallel to the former sea bay and the Jal azZor hills, with most positioned above 18 m a.s.l. Radiocarbon dates concentrate from the end of the 4th millennium to the mid-2nd millennium BC, coinciding with the highest sea levels in Kuwait Bay. The absence of known Bronze Age settlements suggests the burial mounds were constructed by nomadic or semi-nomadic groups with close ties to the sea.
sites.ad: A vast tumulus burial field with 130 stone burial mounds on the northern coast of Kuwait Bay. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) established that tumuli are distributed along terraces parallel to the former sea bay, most above 18 m a.s.l. The absence of known Bronze Age settlements suggests construction by nomadic or semi-nomadic groups with close ties to the sea.
sites.sig: One of the largest Bronze Age burial complexes in the Arabian Gulf. Artefact-based dating spans from Early Dynastic I-II ( 2900 BC) through the Kassite period ( 1150 BC), with possible earlier Ubaid-period origins and later Iron Age reuse.
sites.ex: Kuwaiti-Polish Archaeological Mission (KPAM), directed by Dr. Łukasz Rutkowski
disc: Tumuli with Outer Ring Walls: Impressive dry-stone funerary monuments with distinctive outer ring walls, a construction technique unique to this region.
Semi-Precious Stone Beads: Perforated pearls and beads of carnelian, agate, lapis lazuli, and chrysoprase — evidence of long-distance trade reaching Afghanistan and the Indus Valley.
Dilmun Shell Ornaments: Circular shell plaques with geometric decoration and ‘dot-in-circle’ motifs characteristic of the Umm an-Nar and Dilmun cultures.
Akkadian-Style Cylinder Seal: A cylinder seal dated 2300–2100 BC found between SBH 34 and Bahra 1, connecting the cemetery to Mesopotamian administrative traditions.
Kassite-Style Goblet: A goblet from SBH 34 dated 1600–1150 BC, evidence of continued use of the cemetery into the Late Bronze Age.

sites.desc: A survey in Al-Subiyah identified 21 linear stone platforms along 16 km of coastline, making them the second most common stone structures after tumuli. These platforms are typically 6–21 m long and less than 2 m wide, with rounded ends, flat tops, and a curb of vertical stone slabs. One end is often broader and rounded, while the other resembles a boat’s bow or parabolic tip, giving them a silhouette akin to a longboat or spearhead when viewed from above (Rutkowski & Kiersnowski, 2025).
sites.ad: Boat-shaped stone platforms found along the Al-Subiyah coast, oriented toward the ancient shoreline. These enigmatic structures are unique to the Kuwait Bay region with no direct parallels elsewhere. Their boat-like shape and coastal orientation suggest a ritual or navigational function related to maritime activities or funerary practices.
sites.sig: Their deliberate seaward orientation — perpendicular to the ancient coastline — suggests they were built during the Bronze Age highstand when the sea was visible from their location. They may represent funerary biers, ceremonial podia, or eschatological symbols of passage to the afterlife, evoking Dilmun’s association with paradise in Sumerian mythology.
sites.ex: Kuwaiti-Polish Archaeological Mission (KPAM), 7 excavated by KPAM, 2 by Kuwaiti/GCC teams
disc: Boat-Shaped Silhouette: Elongated platforms with a distinct ‘bow end’ and broader ‘stern end’, resembling longboats when viewed from above — possibly symbolizing the passage to the afterlife.
Sunrise-Sunset Orientation: In the Bahra micro-region, five platforms are aligned east-west with the narrow end pointing westward, possibly reflecting afterlife beliefs.
Fan-Like Coastal Arrangement: Elsewhere, platforms follow a fan-like arrangement perpendicular to the former shoreline, with narrow ends facing the sea.
Association with Tumuli: Often found near tumuli, suggesting functional, ritual, or symbolic associations between the two types of structures.

sites.desc: An isolated shell midden approximately 20×20 m, composed almost exclusively of Conus persicus shells, discovered at the base of Terrace A in the Mughaira area. The site served as a shell processing location for bead production. Nearby finds include Ubaid pottery fragments and flint pieces. KPAM discovered oval quartz pebbles among the shells, resembling the ‘chipped quartz industry’ identified at Bahra 1 and H3 (Rutkowski & Kiersnowski, 2025).
sites.ad: SMQ 24 is a significant shell midden site near Mughaira on the Al-Subiyah coast. Shell middens are ancient refuse heaps primarily composed of discarded mollusk shells, providing invaluable evidence of prehistoric diet, seasonality, and coastal resource exploitation.
sites.sig: Radiocarbon dating yielded a surprisingly late date (Late Bronze Age), suggesting prolonged or intermittent use across different periods. Located 3 km NW of H3 and 5.7 km east of Bahra 1, at a comparable elevation, suggesting potential existence of other Ubaid-period sites along the prehistoric coastline.
disc: Conus persicus Shell Concentration: Thousands of C. persicus shells — the raw material for ancient bead production — concentrated in a 20×20 m area.
Oval Quartz Pebbles: Whole, halved, or fragmented quartz pebbles resembling the ‘chipped quartz industry’ from Bahra 1 and H3, supporting the bead production hypothesis.
Ubaid Pottery Fragment: A fragment of Ubaid pottery found nearby, potentially linking the midden to the Ubaid-period settlements.

sites.desc: Two stone-lined wells along the Al-Subiyah coast, part of a larger network of wellstations along a coastal communication route. SM 12 in Muhaita lies in the path of a wadi from Terrace B; SB 23 in Dubaij lies at the foot of Terrace A. Both feature durable stone linings and auxiliary features (descending steps in SM 12, a water-lifting column in SB 23). Their low elevations indicate they could only function after significant sea regression, placing their construction in the Early Islamic period (Rutkowski & Kiersnowski, 2025).
sites.ad: Two coastal well sites on the Al-Subiyah coast providing evidence of Early Islamic period occupation. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) note these wells became functional 1,200 years ago when a major sea retreat exposed fresh groundwater. Dug into beach rock, they represent the latest phase of human activity in the Al-Subiyah landscape.
sites.sig: Part of a trade or pilgrimage route network extending from Dubaij to Muhaita to Mudaira and Kadhima (30 km further west). The wells’ construction coincides with the rise of Islam and the hajj pilgrimage, possibly serving an alternative coastal route to the main Darb Zubaydah.
disc: Well SM 12 (Muhaita): Stone-lined well with descending steps, positioned in a wadi path to collect rainwater runoff. Remained in use until recent times with modern renovations.
Well SB 23 (Dubaij): Well complex with a water-lifting column and an elongated stone pavement — possibly a large animal drinking trough similar to those found in Kadhima.
Trade Route Evidence: The wells form a network of designated well-stations along a coastal route, with Kadhima (5 animal troughs) as a caravan hub.

sites.desc: Fragments of torpedo jars — elongated storage vessels widely used in the Parthian, Sasanian, and Early Islamic periods in Iraq and southwestern Iran — found scattered along the northern coast of Kuwait Bay from Kadhima in the west to Ras al-Subiyah in the east. These containers were distributed across the western Indian Ocean by sea and discarded after use along former beach strandlines (Rutkowski & Kiersnowski, 2025).
sites.ad: Scatters of distinctive “torpedo jar” pottery along the Al-Subiyah coast. These elongated vessels were the standard shipping containers of the Parthian and Sasanian periods (247 BC – 651 AD), used to transport wine, oil, and commodities across the Persian Gulf trade network.
sites.sig: Evidence of interactions between Mesopotamian seafaring traders and local communities during the late pre-Islamic era. Ceramic analysis indicates at least some jars date to the 5th–6th centuries AD, suggesting the coastline remained accessible until the end of the Sasanian period.
disc: RS 7, RS 10, RS 11 Pottery Scatters: Multiple sites surveyed by KPAM along former beach strandlines in the Ras al-Subiyah area, containing torpedo jar fragments.
RS 8 Stone Mound: A stone mound at 4.10–4.60 m a.s.l. on the same coastal strip as the pottery scatters, possibly a navigation marker.
Sasanian-Period Ceramics: At least some torpedo jars date to the 5th–6th centuries AD, indicating the coastline was still accessible during the Sasanian period.

sites.desc: Kadhima is an Early Islamic settlement located near the western corner of Kuwait Bay. Kennet (2014) documented five animal troughs here, suggesting its role as a caravan hub. Early Islamic settlements dated between the late 7th and mid-9th century AD align with habitation remains in the Mughaira region. The site sits on a potential alternative coastal pilgrimage route to the main Darb Zubaydah (Rutkowski & Kiersnowski, 2025).
sites.ad: Kadhima is historically one of the most important sites in the Persian Gulf. It was a major pre-Islamic trading port and the site of the Battle of Dhat al-Salasil (630 AD), one of the earliest Islamic military campaigns. Its strategic importance stems from its location at the head of Kuwait Bay, where freshwater springs from the Jahra aquifer meet the sea.
sites.sig: A key waypoint on ancient caravan trade routes connecting southern Arabia to Mesopotamia. The discovery of a similar well here reinforces the concept of an interconnected network of well-stations along the Al-Subiyah coast.
disc: Prehistoric Skeleton: The first full prehistoric skeleton found in Kuwait, excavated in 2002 from one of three graves at the site.
Five Animal Troughs: Large stone troughs for watering caravan animals, confirming Kadhima’s role as a major rest stop (Kennet, 2014).
Early Islamic Settlements: Remains dated to the late 7th–mid-9th century AD, coinciding with the rise of Islam and the hajj pilgrimage.

sites.desc: Failaka Island lies approximately 20 km off the Kuwaiti mainland in the Arabian Gulf. It contains some of the richest and most diverse archaeological remains in the Gulf region, spanning from the Bronze Age Dilmun civilization through the Hellenistic period to Late Islamic fishing settlements.
sites.ad: Failaka Island, 20 km off the Kuwait coast, is one of the most archaeologically rich islands in the Persian Gulf. Known as “Ikaros” during the Hellenistic period, it contains remains from the Dilmun civilization (including a temple complex), a Greek fortress from Alexander the Great’s era, and evidence of continuous occupation spanning nearly 4,000 years.
sites.sig: A key node in the Dilmun trade network and later a Hellenistic outpost connected to Alexander the Great’s campaigns; nominated for UNESCO World Heritage status.
sites.ex: Danish, French, Italian, Kuwaiti-Polish, and Kuwaiti-Georgian expeditions (1958–present)
disc: Dilmun Bronze Age Town: The Sa’ad and Sae’ed area contains extensive Dilmun-period remains including temples, residential areas, and stamp seals — on the UNESCO Tentative List.
Hellenistic Buildings: The Al-Qurainiya site yielded Hellenistic courtyard buildings and Greek inscriptions, evidence of the island’s role in Alexander’s eastern campaigns.
Dilmun Stamp Seals: Numerous stamp seals with depictions of local wildlife including gazelles, connecting to the broader Dilmun trade network.
Late Islamic Fishing Settlement: Kharaib el-Desht on the northwestern coast reveals a Late Islamic fishing community with a recently discovered mosque.

sites.desc: Akkaz, also known as Shuwaikh Island, is a former island within Kuwait Bay that has been connected to the mainland through land reclamation. It was recognized as an archaeological site in 1958 by the Danish mission and contains Dilmun-period remains.
sites.ad: Akkaz, also known as Shuwaikh Island, is a former island within Kuwait Bay connected to the mainland through land reclamation. Recognized as an archaeological site in 1958 by the Danish mission, it contains Dilmun-period remains ( 4000–2000 BC).
sites.sig: Part of the Dilmun civilization’s network of settlements controlling Kuwait Bay; one of the earliest identified archaeological sites in Kuwait.

sites.desc: A small drumstick-shaped island in Kuwait Bay, approximately 57 hectares in area and rising only 2 meters above sea level. Umm an Namil contains multi-period archaeological remains spanning from the Dilmun civilization through the Parthian-Characene era.
sites.ad: A small drumstick-shaped island in Kuwait Bay, 57 hectares, rising only 2 m above sea level. Contains multi-period archaeological remains spanning from the Dilmun civilization through the Parthian-Characene era — over 5,000 years of occupation.
sites.sig: Key island in the Dilmun trade network within Kuwait Bay; evidence of continuous occupation from the Bronze Age through the Parthian period.

sites.desc: The Jal Az-Zor escarpment is the most prominent rock exposure in Kuwait, trending NE-SW for over 60 km along the northern side of Kuwait Bay, reaching up to 36 m in height. It exposes the Lower Fars Formation from the Lower to Middle Miocene. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) report marine deposits aged 40 ka and 30 ka now found 10–30 m above sea level, indicating significant tectonic uplift. Amer & Al-Hajeri (2020) demonstrated the escarpment is a product of complex duplex folding and strike-slip tectonics.
sites.ad: The Jal Az-Zor escarpment is a prominent cliff face along the northern shore of Kuwait Bay, rising 145 m above sea level. It exposes a spectacular polychrome geological sequence from the Miocene-age Fars/Ghar Formation through Quaternary deposits. The cliff reveals tilted strata, unconformities, and evidence of tectonic deformation related to the Zagros fold-thrust belt.
sites.sig: The most pronounced geological feature in Kuwait. Tectonic uplift rates of 1.72–2.64 mm/ yr in the Bahra area (driven by the Bahra anticline and Precambrian Hormuz salt tectonics) have raised marine deposits far above their original position, complicating sea-level reconstructions.

sites.desc: The northwestern zone of the Al-Subiyah mud volcano seep complex (MVSC), mapped by Duane et al. (2015) at approximately 29°37.4′N, 48°01.2′E. Z1 contains the most concentrated cluster of mud volcanoes along the coast, situated on the upper tidal flat surface adjacent to remnant flood channels. Features include small craters, abundant gypsum deposits, and skeletal marine fossils. Bedding dip measurements of 10°–60° indicate significant deformation. The zone preserves evidence of focused brine ascent through unconsolidated sediments.
sites.ad: Zone 1 is the most active of three mud volcano zones on the Al-Subiyah coast. Mud volcanoes form when pressurized subsurface fluids (gas, water, mud) breach the surface along fault planes. These features are significant indicators of active tectonic processes and potential hydrocarbon seepage in the Kuwait Bay region.
sites.sig: The densest concentration of mud volcanoes in the Al-Subiyah complex, with the strongest evidence for repeated seepage events. The association with remnant flood channels suggests fluid pathways were controlled by pre-existing drainage patterns.
disc: Dense Mud Volcano Cluster: The highest concentration of mud volcanoes in the MVSC, with multiple overlapping craters and mounds indicating repeated eruption cycles.
Gypsum Deposits: Abundant gypsum crystals and crusts precipitated from hypersaline brines expelled during mud volcano activity.
Skeletal Marine Fossils: Shallow marine fossils entrained in mud volcano ejecta, indicating the source sediments were originally deposited in a marine environment.
Steep Bedding Dips (10°–60°): Highly deformed bedding around vents, with dip angles up to 60° — far exceeding normal depositional angles, confirming forceful fluid injection.

sites.n: Mud Volcano Zone 2 (Z2) — Central Tidal Flat
sites.desc: The central zone of the MVSC, mapped by Duane et al. (2015) at approximately 29°37.0′N, 48°01.5′E. Z2 occupies the Holocene tidal flat between Z1 and Z3, characterized by medium-sized craters, mound formations, and large seismites. A suspected faulted contact runs diagonally (NE–SW) through this zone, separating it from Z3 to the southeast. Bedding measurements (5°–44°) show variable deformation. The zone transitions from tidal flat sediments to a wind-deflated surface inland.
sites.ad: Zone 2 is located on the central tidal flat of the Al-Subiyah coast. This zone features mud volcanoes within the intertidal sabkha environment, where the interaction between tidal processes and subsurface fluid emissions creates unique geomorphological features.
sites.sig: Z2 provides the critical link between the older Z1/Z3 features and active Holocene processes. The faulted contact cutting through this zone suggests ongoing tectonic control on fluid migration, and the seismites here are among the best-preserved earthquake records in soft sediments worldwide.
disc: Large Seismites: Spectacular soft-sediment deformation structures formed by earthquake-triggered liquefaction — some of the best-preserved examples in the Arabian Gulf region.
Suspected Faulted Contact: A diagonal (NE–SW) structural discontinuity mapped by Duane et al. separating Z2 from Z3, suggesting active tectonic control on the distribution of deformation features.
Medium-Sized Craters & Mounds: Intermediate-scale eruption features between the small Z1 craters and the large Z3 craters, suggesting a gradient in subsurface pressure.
Variable Bedding Dips (5°–44°): Wide range of deformation intensities within a single zone, indicating multiple episodes of fluid injection at different pressures.

sites.n: Mud Volcano Zone 3 (Z3) — SE Marine Terrace
sites.desc: The southeastern zone of the MVSC, mapped by Duane et al. (2015) at approximately 29°36.3′N, 48°02.0′E. Z3 sits on the Quaternary marine terrace — older, more consolidated substrate than the Holocene tidal flat of Z2. This zone contains the largest craters, giant seismites, and distinctive polygonal fracture patterns. Bedding dips reach 60° and bioturbation zones are present nearby. Prominent remnant flood channels cut through the zone, and the dense fish-scale pattern of mud volcano features indicates the most intense subsurface fluid activity in the entire complex.
sites.ad: Zone 3 is the southernmost mud volcano zone, located near the coastal sabkha. This zone shows evidence of both active and dormant mud volcanic features, providing insights into the temporal variability of subsurface fluid emissions in the Kuwait Bay area.
sites.sig: Z3 represents the most powerful expressions of subsurface fluid dynamics in the MVSC. The giant seismites and polygonal fractures indicate extreme pore-pressure events, possibly linked to major seismic episodes. Its position on the Quaternary marine terrace means these features have been preserved for tens of thousands of years.
disc: Giant Seismites: The largest soft-sediment deformation structures in the MVSC — massive contorted layers recording powerful seismic events that liquefied the entire sediment column.
Polygonal Fracture Networks: Distinctive geometric fracture patterns formed by desiccation and dewatering of mud volcano ejecta, indicating repeated cycles of eruption and drying.
Large Craters (>2 m diameter): The biggest eruption craters in the complex, formed by violent upward expulsion of fluidized sediment during major seismic or pressure events.
Remnant Flood Channels: Ancient drainage channels that cut through the mud volcano field, suggesting the features pre-date or were contemporaneous with major flooding events.
Bioturbation Zones: Areas of biological reworking adjacent to the mud volcanoes, indicating that organisms colonized the margins of the volcanic field between eruption events.

sites.desc: Extensive hypersaline coastal flats surrounding Kuwait Bay, characterized by evaporitic mineral deposits. Khalaf & Al-Zamel (2014) documented multiple gypcrete types — massive crusts, gypsum roses, rhyzocretes, and powdery crusts. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) note that Iron Age coastal progradation ( 3040 BP) created unfavourable sabkha conditions, contributing to a decline in human activity.
sites.ad: Extensive coastal sabkha deposits along the Al-Subiyah coast, characterized by evaporite minerals (halite, gypsum, anhydrite) formed through repeated cycles of marine flooding and evaporation. These salt flats provide a modern analogue for understanding ancient evaporite sequences in the geological record.
sites.sig: Living geological laboratories for studying evaporite mineral formation. The formation of the sabkha belt in the former bay during the Iron Age created conditions unfavourable for settlement, explaining the archaeological gap in the first millennium BC.

sites.desc: Bou-Rabee, Young & Okal (2020) documented cemented sand and gravel-filled dikes of Pleisto-Holocene age along the Jazirat Dubaij / Jal Az-Zor coast, with appearance and composition similar to typical ‘sandstone pipes.’ The significant age difference between the cemented dikes and surrounding loose sand, their size and spatial distribution, and the local geologic setting suggest they result from a single large event of seismic origin — either shaking during a large earthquake or seiching of tsunami-like waves. The research may help explain the disappearance of an ancient civilization that lived in the region 7,000 years ago.
sites.ad: A field of cemented sand dikes and gravel-filled features in loose PleistoHolocene sand along the Al-Subiyah coast. These paleo-liquefaction features formed when a powerful earthquake shook water-saturated sediments, causing them to behave like liquid. The cemented dikes preserve a record of ancient seismic activity in a region not typically associated with earthquakes.
sites.sig: First documented evidence of prehistoric liquefaction in Kuwait, with major implications for seismic hazard assessment in the Arabian Gulf. The catastrophic event may explain the abandonment of Ubaid-period coastal settlements like H3.
disc: Cemented Sand Dikes: Sandstone pipe-like features where liquefied sand was injected upward through cracks during seismic shaking, then cemented in place.
Sand Boils at Jal Az-Zor: Photographs of sand boils found near the Jazirat Dubaij site, at the Jal Az-Zor escarpment — surface expressions of subsurface liquefaction.

sites.desc: A major dry river valley running 72 km in a NE-SW direction through the AlDibdibah plain, forming the border between Kuwait and Iraq. The wadi is the remnant of an ancient river system that once flowed from Saudi Arabia through Kuwait. Some scholars identify it as the biblical Pishon River. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) note limited evidence of an alternative coastal route serving travellers along this wadi.
sites.ad: Wadi Al-Batin is a major dry river valley forming the western border of Kuwait. Some researchers have proposed it as the biblical “Pishon River” mentioned in Genesis. The wadi was an active river system during wetter Pleistocene climates, draining the interior of the Arabian Peninsula toward Kuwait Bay.
sites.sig: Identified by geologists Juris Zarins and James A. Sauer as the biblical Pishon River; traced via LANDSAT satellite imagery by Farouk El-Baz.

sites.desc: Integrated seismic, petrographic, and noble-gas data reveal deep-seated faults and seismic pipes beneath the Bahrah area that enable hydrothermal fluids to rise from the basement, breaching seals and causing oil leakage, baroque dolomite formation, helium isotope anomalies, and surface sag structures (Behbehani et al., 2019). Bahrah is dynamically linked to basement tectonics and hydrothermal circulation.
sites.ad: The Bahrah hydrothermal system is an area of anomalous geothermal activity in southern Kuwait. Warm springs and elevated ground temperatures indicate deep fluid circulation along fault systems. This is one of the few known hydrothermal systems in the Arabian Peninsula lowlands.
sites.sig: Demonstrates direct coupling between deep crustal processes and surface features in Kuwait — invisible faults act as conduits moving hot fluids from kilometers deep to the surface.

sites.desc: Field mapping by Duane et al. (2015) documented a remarkable assemblage of soft-sediment deformation features in the coastal sabkhas north of Kuwait Bay: mud pillows, fluidized craters, flame structures, and convolute bedding. These formed by earthquake-triggered liquefaction and focused brine ascent through unconsolidated tidal flat sediments.
sites.ad: Deformation structures within sabkha sediments caused by seismic shaking. These seismites include convoluted bedding, flame structures, and sand dikes that formed when earthquake waves passed through water-saturated evaporite deposits. They provide evidence of paleoseismic activity in the Kuwait Bay region.
sites.sig: Kuwait’s tidal flats preserve rare onshore evidence of seismic shaking recorded directly in soft sediments — among the best-preserved examples worldwide.

sites.desc: Radiocarbon dating of marine mollusk shells from the Bahra area by Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) has significantly enhanced understanding of Holocene sea transgression. The earliest transgression at Bahra dates to 7400–7100 cal BP. The long-term highstand included two or three peaks (around 5700 BP and 4000 BP), with sea levels +3.5 m or more above present in the Bahra area. A notable concentration of dates from the end of the 4th millennium to the mid-2nd millennium BC suggests the highest sea levels coincided with the Bronze Age cemetery use. A late pre-Islamic minor highstand ( 2000– 1500 cal BP) temporarily halted regression.
sites.ad: Evidence of Holocene sea-level changes preserved along the Kuwait Bay coastline. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski (2025) documented multiple paleo-shoreline indicators including raised beach deposits, marine terraces, and fossil coral reefs that record the complex history of sea-level fluctuations over the past 10,000 years.
sites.sig: The most comprehensive Holocene sea-level reconstruction for northern Kuwait Bay, integrating neotectonic influences. Demonstrates that the mid-Holocene highstand shaped the entire archaeological landscape — from settlement locations to cemetery placement to ritual platform orientation.

sites.desc: Structural mapping by Naqi & Amer (2021) identifies this section of the Jal Az-Zor escarpment as a ‘Principal Displacement Zone’ — not merely an erosional cliff but an active dextral-slip (right-lateral) fault. The ground is physically moving laterally while also being pushed upward by the Arabian Plate’s collision with Iran. This creates the distinctive ‘step’ in the landscape visible on satellite imagery. The exposed Dammam Formation limestone here shows Eocene marine fossils with significant karst (cave/sinkhole) potential, analogous to the Edwards Plateau in Texas.
sites.ad: A right-lateral (dextral) strike-slip fault identified in the Kuwait Bay region. This fault is part of the broader tectonic framework connecting the Zagros fold-thrust belt to the Arabian Platform. Its identification is significant for seismic hazard assessment in Kuwait.

sites.desc: A high-density fracture field in the Dammam Limestone where recent ‘covercollapse’ sinkholes are actively forming as rainwater exploits vertical joints. Al-Rashed & Al-Sarawi (2018) documented karst features and sinkholes in northern Kuwait, establishing the geological framework. February 2026 field reports document new collapse events within rainwater channels, with deep shadows and cracks trending northeast. The mechanism is identical to cenote formation in the Yucatan Peninsula: the limestone roof of subsurface caverns becomes too thin to support the overlying desert gravels, causing sudden collapse. The Karst Susceptibility Index (KSI) here is among the highest in Kuwait due to steep slopes (>25 degrees), proximity to the main escarpment fault, and high solubility of the Dammam Limestone.
sites.ad: A complex of sinkholes in the Had Safah area formed by dissolution of underlying limestone and gypsum. These karst features represent an active geological hazard and provide evidence of ongoing subsurface dissolution processes in the Kuwait Bay region.
sites.sig: Represents an active geological hazard with implications for infrastructure planning. Also provides a ‘window’ into the subsurface karst system that may connect to deeper aquifer networks. Analogous to the Pennyroyal Plain sinkholes in Kentucky and the Nullarbor Plain in Australia.

sites.desc: The primary outcrop of Kuwait Group gravels containing abundant permineralized (petrified) wood. These fossilized tree limbs were transported by the ancient PaleoBatin river system from the interior of Arabia and buried in fluvial sandstone environments. Diagnostic features include ferruginous (iron-rich) pseudomorphic replacement where original cellulose was replaced by Goethite or Hematite through mineral-rich groundwater seepage. Critically, many specimens contain Teredolite ichnofossils — borings made by marine wood-boring organisms — proving the wood floated in estuarine (brackish) water before burial. This is the ‘smoking gun’ evidence that this area was a massive river delta where fresh river water met the salty ancient Gulf.
sites.ad: A field of permineralized (petrified) wood specimens in northern Kuwait, where ancient tree trunks have been replaced by silica minerals while preserving the original wood structure at cellular level. These fossils indicate that Kuwait once had a much wetter climate supporting forests.
sites.sig: Proves the existence of a major ancient river delta system in northern Kuwait. The Teredolite ichnofossils are globally significant as they demonstrate the transition from fluvial to marine environments. Analogous to the Nubian Sandstone petrified forests of North Africa.

sites.desc: Globally rare vertical sandstone pipes (‘chimneys’) formed when overpressured sand slurry ‘blasted’ through overlying rock layers millions of years ago. Al-Hajeri et al. (2020) documented enigmatic clastic injectite outcrops associated with forced-folds in the Al-Bahrah area. These sand injectites are surface analogues for deep oil and gas reservoir connectivity, making them scientifically valuable to the energy industry. The ‘Martian-red’ iron-stained outcrops at nearby coordinates (29.6141°N, 48.0540°E) are particularly photogenic. Ecologically, these vertical structures create ‘micro-relief’ that traps moisture in an otherwise barren landscape, supporting specialized desert lichen, mosses, and even small shrubs — a rare desert biotope. The zone also exhibits intense vertical fracturing near the cliff edge, with high risk for future sinkhole development.
sites.ad: A unique geological-ecological site where sand injectite features (sand that was forcefully injected into surrounding rock by pressure) coexist with a desert biotope supporting specialized flora and fauna. The injectites formed during seismic events when liquefied sand was injected upward through fractures.
sites.sig: A dual-purpose scientific site: the injectites serve as world-class analogues for subsurface fluid flow (used by petroleum geologists globally), while simultaneously creating rare ecological microhabitats. Analogous to the Panoche Hills Injectite Complex in California.

sites.desc: A ‘Positive Flower Structure’ forms when strike-slip tectonic motion ‘squeezes’ the ground upward, creating a localized topographic high. At these coordinates, a distinctive V-shaped drainage pattern points away from a central high point, which is the diagnostic signature of compressional uplift along a strike-slip fault. This is a smaller-scale version of the pressure ridges found along the San Andreas Fault in California. The structure confirms that the tectonic forces affecting the Jal Az-Zor escarpment extend southwestward into the Jahra area, connecting the two project zones into a single tectonic system.
sites.ad: A positive flower structure is a distinctive tectonic feature formed at a restraining bend along a strike-slip fault. In Kuwait Bay, this structure manifests as an uplifted zone where converging fault strands push rock upward, creating a flower-like cross-sectional profile. It indicates active transpressional tectonics.

sites.desc: Satellite imagery analysis reveals circular, darkened depressions that do not align with natural drainage wadis — the hallmark signature of karst dissolution features. These depressions form where rainwater percolates through fractures in the Dammam Limestone, gradually dissolving the rock and creating subsurface voids. When the roof becomes too thin, the surface collapses. The area shows ‘Green Spot’ anomalies where vegetation grows inside sinkholes due to trapped moisture, providing a natural detection method. Shadow analysis at low sun angles (7:00 AM) reveals additional subtle lineaments and circular features invisible at midday.
sites.ad: An area of karst topography where dissolution of underlying carbonate and evaporite rocks has created a landscape of sinkholes, dolines, and solution channels. This zone is actively monitored as a geological hazard area, with new sinkholes potentially forming as groundwater continues to dissolve bedrock.
sites.sig: Represents a previously unmapped karst field with potential for significant subsurface cavern systems. The ‘Green Spot’ detection method provides a low-cost remote sensing technique for identifying hidden sinkholes across Kuwait’s limestone terrain. Analogous to the Nullarbor Plain in Australia.

sites.n: Jahra Freshwater Lens & Red Palace Wells
sites.desc: Below the Jahra Reserve lies a rare geological ‘hydro-trap’ — a freshwater lens floating on denser saltwater. KISR monitoring studies (2024) track the drawdown of this lens, which is critical for the reserve’s ecology. The historic Red Palace (Qasr Al-Ahmar) was strategically built atop this freshwater source, demonstrating that ancient inhabitants understood the hydrogeology. The lens forms where permeable Quaternary sands overlie impermeable clay layers, creating a natural freshwater reservoir in an otherwise arid, saline environment.
sites.ad: The Jahra freshwater lens is a critical hydrogeological feature — a body of fresh groundwater floating atop denser saline water beneath the Jahra coastal plain. This lens sustained the historic Red Palace wells and the Jahra oasis, making it the foundation of human settlement in the area for millennia.
sites.sig: Explains why Jahra has been continuously inhabited for millennia — it sits atop one of Kuwait’s few natural freshwater sources. The freshwater lens is the hydrological engine driving the entire Jahra wetland ecosystem.

sites.desc: This zone hosts Halocnemum strobilaceum, a remarkable ‘biological sensor’ plant whose health directly indicates groundwater salinity levels. The plant survives extreme conditions by sequestering salt in specialized leaf structures, which eventually drop and enrich the surrounding soil. The halophytic succession here follows a precise gradient from the most salt-tolerant species near the coast to less tolerant species inland, creating a living map of the subsurface salinity profile. Acacias and Tamarisks in the reserve act as a natural phytoremediation system, filtering excess nitrates and phosphates from treated water before it reaches the marine mudflats.
sites.ad: A well-defined halophytic plant succession zone along the Jahra coast, where salt-tolerant plant species arrange themselves in distinct bands based on salinity gradients. This ecological zonation demonstrates how plants adapt to extreme saline conditions, from bare sabkha to dense halophyte meadows.
sites.sig: A living laboratory for studying plant adaptation to extreme salinity. The halophytic gradient serves as a biological proxy for mapping invisible groundwater chemistry, and the phytoremediation function protects the marine ecosystem downstream.

sites.desc: This is a high-resolution nesting site for the globally threatened Basra Reed Warbler (Acrocephalus griseldis). Census data shows that the density of nesting pairs here is among the highest in the Middle East, directly linked to the specific height (2.5–3 meters) of the Phragmites reeds. The site is part of a broader avian corridor: recent satellite tracking (2023–2025) of the Greater Spotted Eagle shows that raptors use thermal updrafts created by the Jal Az-Zor ridge to the north, then ‘drop in’ to the Jahra Reserve for hydration — making this area literally a ‘gas station’ for international migratory travelers.
sites.ad: A critical breeding habitat for the Basra Reed Warbler (Acrocephalus griseldis), classified as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. This small pocket of reed beds along the Jahra coast represents one of the southernmost breeding sites for this species, which is primarily found in the marshes of southern Iraq.

sites.desc: A natural depression (Khabra) where seasonal moisture collects, creating a ‘Biological Refugia’ — a pocket of life that survives because the underlying clay layers hold rainwater like a bowl. During the brief spring season, Desert Iris and native grasses bloom here, creating a striking green anomaly visible on satellite imagery (high NDVI signature). The depression also marks a sharp change in the strike direction of the escarpment ridge, with a high Sinuosity Index indicating tectonic deformation rather than simple wind erosion. This makes the Khabra both a botanical wonder and a structural geology indicator.
sites.ad: A seasonal playa (dry lake bed) that transforms into a meadow of wild irises after winter rains. This ephemeral ecosystem demonstrates the remarkable resilience of desert flora, with iris bulbs surviving underground through extreme summer heat to bloom spectacularly each spring.
sites.sig: Demonstrates how geology controls ecology: the clay-lined depression is a product of differential erosion along a fault bend, and the trapped water creates a micro-ecosystem in the desert. Analogous to the Playa Lakes of the Texas High Plains.

sites.desc: Dr. Sarah Al-Ateeqi’s research documents the ecological footprint of the Sabriya Oil Field in northern Kuwait. The study reveals how decades of hydrocarbon extraction have created a unique industrial-ecological interface where native desert flora and fauna adapt to chronic lowlevel contamination. Soil sampling shows elevated heavy metal concentrations (Cd, Pb, Cr, Ni) in a gradient pattern radiating from wellheads and gathering centers. Remarkably, certain halophytic species (Zygophyllum qatarense, Haloxylon salicornicum) show phytoremediation capacity, accumulating metals in their tissues. The site demonstrates both the environmental cost of oil production and nature’s resilience.

sites.desc: The Bahra area, famous for its archaeological sites, also hosts a distinctive desert ecosystem studied by Dr. Al-Ateeqi. The transition zone between the coastal sabkha and inland desert creates a unique ecological gradient. Soil analysis reveals that the ancient Ubaid-period occupation layers have altered the soil chemistry, creating ‘anthropogenic soil islands’ with higher organic content and different microbial communities compared to surrounding virgin desert. These enriched patches support denser vegetation, creating a visible ‘green halo’ effect around archaeological sites — a phenomenon that could aid remote sensing detection of undiscovered sites.

sites.desc: Um Al-Aish is a critical wetland area in northern Kuwait where Dr. Al-Ateeqi’s research focuses on the interaction between groundwater discharge and surface ecology. The site features seasonal marshes fed by shallow aquifer seepage, creating a rare freshwater-to-brackish gradient in the desert. The wetland supports a surprisingly diverse invertebrate community including dragonflies, water beetles, and freshwater snails — species typically absent from Kuwait’s arid landscape. The area also serves as a stopover for migratory waterbirds on the Central Asian Flyway, with recent surveys recording over 40 bird species during peak migration.

sites.desc: The Sabah Al-Ahmad Natural Reserve is Kuwait’s largest protected area, spanning over 330 km². Dr. Al-Ateeqi’s research here focuses on ecosystem recovery following protection from grazing and off-road vehicle damage. Long-term vegetation monitoring plots show that native perennial grasses (Stipagrostis plumosa, Panicum turgidum) have increased by 340% since protection began, while invasive species have declined. The reserve also hosts reintroduced Arabian oryx and sand gazelle populations. Soil crust studies reveal that biological soil crusts (cyanobacteria, mosses, lichens) — destroyed by decades of overgrazing — are slowly reforming, stabilizing the soil and reducing dust emissions.

sites.desc: The Burgan Oil Field — the world’s second-largest oil field — suffered catastrophic environmental damage during the 1991 Gulf War when over 700 oil wells were set ablaze. Dr. Al-Ateeqi’s research documents the 35-year ecological recovery trajectory. Soil contamination from oil lakes and soot fallout created a ‘dead zone’ that is slowly being recolonized by pioneer species. Remarkably, certain areas show accelerated recovery where oil-degrading bacteria (Pseudomonas, Bacillus) have naturally bioaugmented the soil. The research also tracks heavy metal (V, Ni, Cr) bioaccumulation in desert plants growing on contaminated soil, providing critical data for human health risk assessment.

sites.desc: The Umm Gudair oil field in southwestern Kuwait represents one of the most extreme arid environments in the country. Dr. Al-Ateeqi’s research here examines how oil field infrastructure (pipelines, roads, gathering centers) inadvertently creates microhabitats for desert wildlife. Pipeline berms trap windblown sand and moisture, creating linear ‘oases’ where vegetation density is 5x higher than surrounding desert. These green corridors serve as movement pathways for desert foxes, hedgehogs, and dhub lizards. The study also documents the impact of gas flaring on nocturnal insect behavior, with moths and beetles attracted to flare stacks from distances exceeding 10 km.

sites.desc: The Um Al-Rros area in western Kuwait hosts military training grounds where Dr. Al-Ateeqi’s research examines the ecological impact of military vehicle traffic on desert soil and vegetation. Heavy tracked vehicles compact the desert surface, destroying the biological soil crust and creating ‘deflation hollows’ where wind erosion accelerates. However, abandoned tank berms and foxholes from the 1991 Gulf War have inadvertently become wildlife refugia — the depressions trap rainwater and windblown seeds, creating micro-ecosystems. Desert monitors (Varanus griseus) and spiny-tailed lizards (Uromastyx aegyptia) preferentially use old military structures for thermoregulation and nesting.

sites.desc: Satellite imagery reveals several dark reddish-brown circular mound features (10– 30 m diameter) on the lighter desert surface south of Subiyah. These features are distinctly different from the surrounding terrain in both color and texture, appearing as a loose cluster. The surrounding terrain shows lighter patches of possible gypcrete or salt crust, while the mounds themselves are anomalously dark — suggesting iron-oxide staining, bitumen seepage, or cemented sand from paleo-liquefaction events.
sites.ad: AI-detected dark circular mounds on satellite imagery that may represent active hydrocarbon or fluid seepage features. These speculative features require ground-truthing but could indicate subsurface petroleum migration pathways, similar to seepage mounds documented in other parts of the Arabian Gulf.
sites.sig: If confirmed as fluid seepage features, these mounds would extend the known footprint of Behbehani et al.‘s (2019) deep-fault hydrothermal system southward, demonstrating that basementto-surface fluid migration is more widespread than previously documented. Alternatively, if they are paleo-liquefaction features, they would expand the spatial extent of Bou-Rabee et al.’s (2020) prehistoric earthquake evidence.
sites.ev: Satellite imagery shows distinct dark circular features (10–30 m) on lighter desert surface. Color and morphology are inconsistent with aeolian or sabkha processes. Located in the structural corridor between known hydrothermal (Behbehani) and liquefaction (Bou-Rabee) sites.
sites.an: Similar dark seepage mounds are documented at the Bahrah oil seep area (Behbehani et al., 2019) and at onshore mud volcano sites in Azerbaijan’s Absheron Peninsula, where subsurface fluids stain surface sediments.
sites.val: Ground-truth visit to check for hydrocarbon odor or mineral crusts. Portable XRF analysis of the dark material. Shallow auger drilling to test for cemented sand or bitumen. Helium soil gas survey following Behbehani et al.‘s methodology.

sites.desc: At the Jal Az-Zor escarpment face, satellite imagery reveals dramatic multicolored terrain that is highly unusual for Kuwait’s typically monochrome desert. Bright orange-red terrain grades into grey-purple patches and white-cream bands, with the color zonation following the topographic contours of the escarpment. Dendritic drainage channels cut into the terrain, exposing different colored layers. This polychrome pattern suggests either differential weathering of distinct geological formations or, more intriguingly, hydrothermal alteration of the rock by ascending fluids.
sites.ad: An AI-detected section of the Jal Az-Zor escarpment showing unusually vivid polychrome banding that may indicate previously undocumented mineral assemblages or alteration zones. The enhanced color variation could represent hydrothermal alteration, iron oxide enrichment, or unusual diagenetic processes.
sites.sig: If the orange-red coloration is confirmed as iron-oxide staining from hydrothermal fluids, this would provide surface evidence of the deep-fault fluid migration system described by Behbehani et al. (2019) manifesting at the Jal Az-Zor escarpment — a location not previously identified as part of this system. The escarpment could serve as a natural geological cross-section exposing the fluid pathways.
sites.ev: Satellite imagery shows dramatic color variations (orange-red, grey-purple, white-cream) at the escarpment face. The color banding follows topographic contours. The orange-red is inconsistent with typical aeolian deposits and suggests iron-oxide enrichment.
sites.an: Similar polychrome escarpment exposures are seen at Jebel Hafeet (UAE) and in the Zagros Mountains (Iran), where different geological formations and hydrothermal alteration create a ‘layer cake’ of colors visible from satellite.
sites.val: Geological mapping traverse along the escarpment face with systematic rock sampling. XRD/XRF analysis to identify mineral composition of each color zone. Thin-section petrography to check for hydrothermal alteration minerals (e.g., hematite, goethite, kaolinite).

sites.desc: In the shallow waters off the western Kuwait Bay coast near Kathma, satellite imagery reveals a large dark oval feature approximately 200 m across, distinctly darker than the surrounding shallow water. The feature sits on a clear paleoshoreline transition zone where the desert surface meets the tidal flat. The water color gradients show beautiful bathymetric detail — turquoise for very shallow areas grading to dark blue for deeper water — and this dark feature stands out as anomalous against the lighter shallow-water background.
sites.ad: An AI-detected dark anomaly on the seafloor near the ancient port of Kathma (Kadhima). This submerged feature could represent a sunken archaeological site, a natural geological formation, or an area of active fluid seepage. Its proximity to the historically important Kadhima port makes it a high-priority target for underwater investigation.
sites.sig: Kathma (Kadhima) is historically one of the most important sites in the Gulf — it was a major pre-Islamic trading port and the site of the Battle of Dhat al-Salasil (630 AD). If this submerged feature is archaeological, it could represent remains of the ancient harbor infrastructure or a submerged settlement from when sea levels were different. If geological, it could be an exposed bedrock outcrop of the Dammam Formation on the seabed.
sites.ev: Satellite imagery shows a discrete dark oval ( 200 m) in shallow water near the historically significant Kathma coast. The feature is morphologically distinct from surrounding seabed. Located at a paleoshoreline transition zone.
sites.an: Similar dark submerged features near known archaeological coasts have been identified as submerged settlement remains at Dwarka (India) and Pavlopetri (Greece). In the Gulf, submerged Neolithic sites have been found off Abu Dhabi.
sites.val: Snorkeling or diving survey at low tide to visually inspect the feature. Side-scan sonar to map the seabed morphology. If solid material is found, sediment cores for dating. Drone-based bathymetric LiDAR for high-resolution depth mapping.

sites.desc: Satellite imagery reveals a large submerged shallow platform extending northwest from Failaka Island. The water color gradients clearly show a broad area of very shallow water (turquoisegreen) with a sharp drop-off to deeper water (dark blue) to the west and north. The platform has an irregular but roughly arcuate shape. On the adjacent Failaka coast, the Tal Sa’ida Archaeological Site and other antiquities markers confirm the area’s archaeological significance. During the early Holocene when sea level was approximately 15 m lower than present, this entire platform would have been dry land — potentially forming a land bridge or near-connection between Failaka and the mainland.
sites.ad: An AI-detected submerged platform feature near Failaka Island that may represent a drowned coastal terrace or anthropogenic structure. Given Failaka’s 4,000-year archaeological record, this feature could be related to ancient harbor infrastructure or a natural marine terrace from a previous sea-level highstand.
sites.sig: This submerged platform may preserve evidence of early Holocene human occupation or migration routes. Rutkowski & Kiersnowski’s (2025) sea-level curve shows that around 8000 BP, sea level was low enough for this platform to be exposed. The Ubaid-period settlers at Bahra 1 (across the bay) could have used this land connection. Any archaeological remains on the platform would predate the known Dilmun-era sites on Failaka by thousands of years.
sites.ev: Satellite imagery shows clear bathymetric contrast between a large shallow platform (turquoise) and surrounding deep water (dark blue). The platform extends NW from Failaka where multiple archaeological sites exist. Sea-level reconstructions confirm this area was exposed during early Holocene human occupation.
sites.an: Similar drowned coastal platforms with archaeological significance include the Doggerland between Britain and Europe, the Sunda Shelf in Southeast Asia, and submerged Neolithic sites off the coast of Israel (Atlit-Yam).
sites.val: Multibeam bathymetric survey to map the platform’s detailed morphology. Subbottom profiler to identify buried sediment layers. Grab samples or vibrocores for sediment dating. If shallow enough, systematic diving survey for archaeological material.

sites.desc: Bubiyan Island’s western surface displays an extraordinary network of tidal creeks and channels visible on satellite imagery. Dense dendritic tidal creek patterns cover the entire flat surface, appearing as darker lines against the tan-pink sabkha. Some channels appear to be abandoned and filled while others remain active. A prominent darker band running east-west across the surface may represent a paleoshoreline or geological contact. This network preserves a multi-layered record of tidal processes operating at different sea-level stages during the Holocene.
sites.ad: An AI-detected paleo-tidal channel system on Bubiyan Island visible in satellite imagery. These ancient channels may represent former tidal pathways that were active when sea levels were different, providing evidence of the island’s geomorphological evolution as part of the Shatt Al-Arab delta system.
sites.sig: The abandoned tidal creeks on Bubiyan could preserve a continuous record of Holocene sea-level changes. During the highstand (+2–3.5 m, 6000–4000 BP per Rutkowski & Kiersnowski), much more of Bubiyan would have been submerged. The current tidal creek pattern may overprint older channel systems from different sea-level stages, creating a palimpsest that can be ‘read’ through careful geomorphological analysis. This would provide independent validation of the sea-level curve derived from the Al-Subiyah coast.
sites.ev: Satellite imagery shows dense dendritic tidal creek patterns with both active and abandoned channels. A prominent E-W dark band suggests a paleoshoreline. The multi-generation creek network is consistent with sea-level fluctuations documented by Rutkowski & Kiersnowski.
sites.an: Similar paleotidal creek networks have been used to reconstruct Holocene sealevel histories on the Trucial Coast (UAE), in the Mesopotamian marshes (Iraq), and on the Ranns of Kutch (India).
sites.val: High-resolution drone survey to map active vs. abandoned creek channels. Sediment cores at creek intersections to date different channel generations. OSL dating of abandoned channel fills. Comparison with Rutkowski & Kiersnowski’s sea-level curve to correlate channel abandonment with sea-level drops.
